checks.invariant: DELETE /sandboxes/{sid} is an authoritative revocation: after it reports success the row stays deleted, the old agent token stays invalid, and no concurrent lifecycle request may resurrect the record or its container
checks.result: Violated. restore_sandbox and delete_sandbox are two unlocked read-modify-write sequences on the same sandboxes row (service.py:462-475, sandbox.py:387-401, 320-332). With a deterministic schedule that lets the DELETE finish while the restore is between _rec and its final _set, delete reported success and audited sandbox_delete, then the restore's _set wrote status=running and the new container_id back over it. Observed afterwards: status 'running', container c2 alive, sandboxes.token_matches(sid, old_token)=true, sandbox_for_token(old_token)=sid, snapshot row still present, and POST tools/list_dir with the revoked token returned 200 executed. Sequential control (delete, then restore) failed with ImageNotFound and left status 'deleted' with the token invalid, so the normal path is protected only by best-effort image cleanup (sandbox.py:328-332) which the racing restore itself defeats by keeping the image in use.

checks.invariant: The intended control for a deleted sandbox is an explicit status check (sandbox.py:225-232 _container rejects status=='deleted'; token_matches/sandbox_for_token at 211-223 filter status!='deleted'), and every lifecycle operation must apply it
checks.result: SandboxManager.restore is the one lifecycle operation that reads the row directly with _rec (sandbox.py:388, which returns deleted rows unfiltered) and never checks status, so it can set status back to 'running' (sandbox.py:398). delete and snapshot go through _container or _rec only; pause/resume reject deleted rows through _container. The gate therefore rests on _rec callers remembering the check, not on a shared choke point.

checks.invariant: restore_sandbox validates snapshot_id before it mutates any observable state (ordering of log_human, end_desktop, sandboxes.restore, bursts.reset_timers, log_human)
checks.result: Violated in ordering: service.py:464 runs end_desktop before sandbox.restore validates snap_id (sandbox.py:388-391). With an installed human takeover lease, restore_sandbox(sid, 'snap_bogus') dropped the lease (desktop.close_all at desktop.py:274-280) and wrote a human_handback audit row with reason sandbox_restored, then raised SandboxError. The sandbox itself was untouched (status still running).

checks.invariant: Queued work for a deleted sandbox cannot execute later (retention/queued-work overrun): pending approvals must not outlive DELETE
checks.result: delete_sandbox (service.py:471-475) does not expire approvals. A pending approval for the deleted sid stayed status=pending after DELETE. It is not executable: decide() -> _snapshot -> sandbox.snapshot -> _container raises 'deleted sandbox', the approval is finished as failed and the caller gets 503 (observed: ServiceError 503, final status 'failed'). No agent-controlled execution survived the delete; only a stale, un-actionable card remains until approval_timeout expires it.

checks.invariant: GUI burst records and snapshot timers are closed/rebound across pause, resume, restore and delete so that a later GUI input never runs without a baseline bound to the current container
checks.result: Ordering is correct: pause logs, calls bursts.end then pause (service.py:444-448); restart timers only after resume (450-454); restore closes the burst via end_desktop before the container is replaced and resets timers after (462-469); delete ends the burst before removing the container (471-474). bursts.end cannot raise: GuiBursts._finish catches container replacement and manifest failures into gui_burst_close_failed (gui_bursts.py:113-135), and open binds the burst to container_id (65-77) so a post-restore burst cannot be judged against the pre-restore file/pid lists.

checks.invariant: The audit pairing 'human_takeover has a matching human_handback' survives delete/restore, including when the handback audit write fails
checks.result: end_desktop (service.py:579-587) swallows the ServiceError that _handback_locked raises when the human_handback audit append fails (528-542); the lease is then released by desktop.close_all (desktop.py:274-280), which deletes the takeover_leases row. recover_takeovers (service.py:555-565) only logs leftovers still in that table, so the missing pairing is not repaired. The gap needs an AuditWriteError during delete/restore; on the normal path the pairing is written.

checks.invariant: pause_sandbox ends the human desktop lease like delete/restore do
checks.result: pause_sandbox does not call end_desktop: a takeover lease and its control WebSocket survive a pause of the frozen container and remain after resume. No approval or tool path is freed by the lease, so nothing escalates; the only effect is that agent GUI tools keep getting 423 and the lease outlives a frozen desktop. Recorded as hardening, not a finding.

checks.invariant: UI lifecycle routes use the same human authority and session attribution as the JSON API
checks.result: web.py:245-261 routes take_snapshot/restore/delete through browser_human (screen_human, scope '*') and pass p.session into the service call, so only a scope-'*' human session can drive them and the audit row carries the session. A desktop-link session (scope = one sid) is rejected before the service method.

checks.invariant: The deployment path cannot start the control plane plaintext-exposed or on a runc sandbox runtime without an explicit operator flag (no weaker layer overrides the serve-time gates)
checks.result: Dockerfile:17 starts 'agentbox serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765 --behind-tls-proxy', so bind_problem passes only via behind_tls_proxy and runtime_problem sees exposed=True (cli.py:95-111). compose uses expose: 8765 (docker-compose.yml:29-30) and never publishes the port, only Caddy publishes 80/443 (38-40); AGENTBOX_ALLOW_RUNC defaults to empty (25), so no dev-only override is pre-set. Settings.runtime comes only from the launcher environment (config.py:31) and POST /sandboxes accepts only source_dir/template (api.py:46-48), so no agent/session principal can pick the runtime or the bind.

checks.invariant: Every application entrypoint applies the same bind/TLS and runtime gates
checks.result: create_app (api.py:376-378) calls build() directly and is advertised as a supported entrypoint ('uvicorn agentbox.api:create_app --factory'), so it skips bind_problem and runtime_problem entirely; secure_cookie then comes only from AGENTBOX_SECURE_COOKIE (config.py:69) and the runtime stays whatever _detect_runtime picked. Only the launcher can choose that entrypoint, so this is a hardening note rather than a boundary crossing, but it is a real second path with weaker controls.

checks.invariant: runtime_problem decides on the isolation class of the selected runtime, not on one literal name
checks.result: Revalidated the run-3 rejected claim against current source: cli.py:80 still compares the runtime name to the literal 'runc' while _detect_runtime (sandbox.py:172-182) returns any name Docker lists, so a registered runc-class alias still passes. Source and rejection ground are unchanged (the selector is the launcher environment only), so there is no changed evidence to re-report; the prior rejection stands.

checks.invariant: Proxy-header trust is limited to the proxy that terminates TLS
checks.result: Caddyfile:4-5 reverse-proxies agentbox:8765 and Caddy sets Host/X-Forwarded-Proto; cli.py:126 defaults forwarded_allow_ips to '*' behind --behind-tls-proxy. Because compose only exposes 8765 on the compose network, the only source-visible peer that can forge X-Forwarded-Proto is another container on that network; if the port is ever published, the header becomes attacker-settable and secure_cookie/scheme decisions follow it. No source-visible exposure; owner-observed check recorded in hardening.

candidates.title: A restore racing a delete resurrects the deleted sandbox record and re-authorizes the agent token the delete revoked
candidates.description: DELETE /sandboxes/{sid} and POST /sandboxes/{sid}/restore both perform an unlocked read-modify-write on the same sandboxes row. When a delete lands between the restore's row read and the restore's final status write, the delete reports success and audits 'sandbox_delete', but the restore then writes status='running' and the replacement container_id back over the deleted row. The row's original token_hash is untouched, so the agent token that the delete was supposed to revoke resolves to the sandbox again and tool calls execute; the snapshot row and image also survive the delete (the running replacement container keeps the image in use, so the best-effort image removal is swallowed). The control plane thus reports a completed deletion while the sandbox, its /workspace and its agent authority are still live.
candidates.root_cause: Lifecycle operations take no per-sandbox lock and re-read nothing: Service.restore_sandbox and Service.delete_sandbox (service.py:462-475) call SandboxManager.restore and SandboxManager.delete (sandbox.py:387-401, 320-332), which each read the row once with _rec, act, and write status/container_id unconditionally. SandboxManager.restore never checks status=='deleted', so its final _set (sandbox.py:398) overwrites the delete's status write (sandbox.py:326) and reinstates the record. Revocation of the agent token is expressed only as status!='deleted' (sandbox.py:216, 221), so the overwritten status silently re-authorizes the old token.
candidates.intended_behavior: _container (sandbox.py:225-232) and the token lookups (sandbox.py:211-223) treat status=='deleted' as final: a deleted sandbox is unusable and its agent token is invalid. DELETE is the revocation contract (service.py:471-475 logs sandbox_delete, ends the desktop, deletes the container, drops captures). No later or concurrent lifecycle call may reinstate the record, re-point it at a container, or make the revoked token valid again.

trace.description: human_only route hands the client-supplied snapshot_id to box.restore_sandbox with no serialization against other lifecycle calls
calls SandboxManager.restore outside any lock, after end_desktop has already run
reads the row with _rec, which returns deleted rows too, and never checks status
force-removes the old container, then the long step follows
starts the replacement container from the snapshot image while no lock protects the row
second human request for the same sid runs concurrently on the Starlette threadpool
snapshot image removal fails because the restore's new running container uses the image; APIError is swallowed, so the row and image survive
final _set overwrites the deleted status with status='running' and the new container_id
only rejects status=='deleted', so the original agent token hash is accepted again
resolves the revoked token back to the sid, which api.principal turns into an agent principal

evidence.description: restore_sandbox ordering: log, end_desktop, sandboxes.restore, bursts.reset_timers, log - no lock is acquired, unlike call_tool's _snap_locks
delete_sandbox ordering: log, end_desktop, sandboxes.delete, drop_captures - no lock, so it can interleave with restore
_rec returns the row for any sid including deleted ones, so restore's first read succeeds after a delete
_container is the intended choke point that rejects status=='deleted' for every other operation; restore bypasses it by using _rec directly
delete: read row, remove container, set status='deleted', then best-effort image removal with APIError swallowed
restore: read row, remove old container, run new container, then unconditionally set container_id and status='running'
token_matches expresses revocation only as status != 'deleted'
sandbox_for_token uses the same status filter, so the reauthorization reaches api.principal (api.py:121-123)

conditions.description: Both requests need the human token or a browser session with scope '*'; the agent never issues them, but it holds the agt_ token that DELETE is supposed to revoke and needs no new credential.

A DELETE for the same sid must be in flight while the restore is between its row read and its final status write. The restore path is by far the longer one (end_desktop burst close, container removal, docker run), so a delete issued during a restore normally writes its status first and is then overwritten.
The sandbox has at least one snapshot row; DELETE never removes snapshots rows (sandbox.py:328-332 only tries to remove images), and restore accepts any row of that sid.

No special runtime or container capability is needed: the resurrection is decided entirely in the control plane's SQLite row and token lookups. The image must be present or in use when the replacement container starts; the racing restore keeps it in use.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of the agent token (agt_...) whose authority the human tried to revoke with DELETE. No new credential is needed: after the overlapping restore the same token maps to the sid again and its tool calls return 200.
payloads: DELETE /sandboxes/sb_54e49093  (issued while the restore is between _rec and its final _set)
POST /sandboxes/sb_54e49093/tools/list_dir {"args": {"path": "/workspace"}} with Authorization: Bearer <the agt_ token DELETE was meant to revoke>
instructions: Bounded local harness in the approved sbx sandbox (no network, no Docker daemon): real agentbox.config.Settings, agentbox.audit.AuditLog, agentbox.approvals.ApprovalStore, agentbox.policy.Policy, agentbox.desktop.DesktopControl, agentbox.service.AgentBox and agentbox.sandbox.SandboxManager with a temporary SQLite file under /scratch.

Docker is replaced by a fake client that models the daemon facts this check needs: containers.run registers the name and image and refuses a duplicate container name, images.remove refuses while a container is running on the image (real docker cannot force-remove an image in use), and running an absent image raises ImageNotFound (confirmed by the sequential control run).

Create a cli-template sandbox with an empty source dir, take one snapshot (docker commit is faked into the image set), then start box.restore_sandbox(sid, snap) on a thread. A run() hook parks the restore after the new container exists; the main thread then runs box.delete_sandbox(sid) to completion and releases the restore.

Read back: sandboxes.get(sid)['status'], container_id, sandboxes.token_matches(sid, old_token), sandboxes.sandbox_for_token(old_token), box.call_tool(sid, 'list_dir', {'path': '/workspace'}) with the old token's sandbox, and the audit event list.
Sequential control in the same run: create, snapshot, delete, then restore - it fails with ImageNotFound and leaves status 'deleted' with the token invalid.
execution.observed_result: Race run: delete returned success and audited 'sandbox_delete'; restore then returned normally and audited 'restored'. Read-back: status 'running', container_id c2, container alive, old_token_valid true, token_maps_to_sid true, snapshot rows still present (1), and POST tools/list_dir with the revoked token returned 200 {'status': 'executed', 'result': {'path': '/workspace', 'listing': 'total 0'}}. Audit sequence for the race: sandbox_created, restore_request, sandbox_delete, restored, tool_request. Sequential control: ImageNotFound 'no such image: agentbox-snap:sb_54e49093-snap_b2f2d73f', status 'deleted', token invalid.

remediation.strategy: Serialize all lifecycle transitions per sandbox and make deletion final at the point of the check. Take one per-sid lifecycle lock in AgentBox for pause/resume/snapshot/restore/delete (reusing the _snap_locks map with a distinct key) so delete and restore cannot interleave, and have SandboxManager.restore re-read the row under that lock and refuse status=='deleted' before it removes the old container or starts the replacement. Regression case: drive restore and delete concurrently with the harness and assert that the row is either deleted with the old token invalid and no replacement container, or restored and still deleted=false only if no delete was observed.

code_changes.fixed_code:
def _lifecycle_lock(self, sid: str) -> threading.Lock:
        with self._busy_lock:
            return self._snap_locks.setdefault("lifecycle:" + sid, threading.Lock())

    def restore_sandbox(self, sid: str, snap_id: str, session: str | None = _NO_SESSION) -> dict[str, Any]:
        with self._lifecycle_lock(sid):
            self.log_human("restore_request", sid, _with_session({"snapshot_id": snap_id}, session))
            self.end_desktop(sid, "sandbox_restored")
            rec = self.sandboxes.restore(sid, snap_id)
            self.bursts.reset_timers(sid)
            self.log_human("restored", sid, _with_session({"snapshot_id": snap_id, "container_id": rec["container_id"]}, session))
            return rec

    def delete_sandbox(self, sid: str, session: str | None = _NO_SESSION) -> None:
        with self._lifecycle_lock(sid):
            self.log_human("sandbox_delete", sid, _with_session({}, session))
            self.end_desktop(sid, "sandbox_deleted")
            self.sandboxes.delete(sid)
            self.drop_captures(sid)

likelihood.reason: The two requests must overlap and both need human authority; but when a delete is issued during a restore of the same sandbox the delete's status write is the fast one and the restore's final write lands after it, so the overlap produces the resurrection rather than an error.

impact.reason: Revocation is silently undone: the agent token invalidated by DELETE authorizes tool calls again on a sandbox the human was told was deleted, its /workspace stays writable, and snapshot rows plus the image survive, while the audit log records sandbox_delete followed by restored.

confidence.reason: The control-plane logic and the full source trace are certain and were reproduced deterministically, but the harness models the Docker daemon; the live run at real docker-run latency (parent Phase 3) should confirm the overlap window and the image-in-use behavior.

hardening: restore_sandbox mutates desktop state before the snapshot_id is validated (service.py:464 vs sandbox.py:388-391): an invalid snap_id dropped the human takeover lease and wrote a human_handback row with reason 'sandbox_restored' for a restore that never happened. Validate the snapshot id first, then end the desktop.

SandboxManager.restore force-removes the old container before creating the replacement (sandbox.py:392-397) and does not catch docker ImageNotFound/APIError, so a failed restore leaves the row pointing at a removed container with status 'running' and raises a 500 instead of a SandboxError. Mark the sandbox failed or recreate before removing.

restore and delete keep the intent audit row (restore_request / sandbox_delete) even when the operation is rejected, so DELETE of an unknown sid leaves an audit event that reads as a deletion. Add a paired failure event.

end_desktop swallows the 503 that _handback_locked raises when the human_handback append fails (service.py:579-587) and desktop.close_all then deletes the takeover_leases row (desktop.py:274-280), so recover_takeovers cannot repair the unpaired human_takeover.

delete_sandbox does not expire pending approvals for the sid; the card stays pending until approval_timeout and an approval attempt then consumes it as failed with 503 (observed). Expire them in delete_sandbox next to drop_captures.

pause_sandbox does not call end_desktop, so a takeover lease and its control WebSocket survive a pause and the frozen desktop keeps returning 423 for agent GUI tools until the lease is released or goes stale.

create_app (api.py:376-378) is a documented entrypoint that skips bind_problem and runtime_problem entirely; if it is ever used for a real deployment the TLS and runtime gates are absent. Either route the factory through the same checks or drop the --factory hint.

Behind --behind-tls-proxy, forwarded_allow_ips defaults to '*' (cli.py:126). compose does not publish 8765, so no source-visible peer can forge X-Forwarded-Proto, but the setting should pin the proxy address; owner-observed check: confirm the control-plane port is unreachable except from the Caddy container.

DELETE leaves snapshots rows in the SQLite database (and, when image removal fails, the image itself) plus the per-sandbox sources/{sid} directory for empty-source sandboxes; retention after delete rather than disk pressure, so no unit owns it.

uncovered.surface: DELETE /sandboxes/{sid} retention of derived copies (snapshots table rows, snapshot images when removal fails, home/sources/{sid})
uncovered.boundary: agentbox/sandbox.py#delete row/image cleanup + agentbox/sandbox.py#create empty-source dir
uncovered.reason: The peer disk unit covers pressure on the host, not the lifecycle guarantee that a deleted sandbox's derived copies are gone; a dedicated unit should decide what delete must remove and whether a deleted sid may ever be restored.
